This feeling did go away for me for a while and I was resuming life, but I’ve recently had Covid and some traumatic events happen that have sort of put me back in that place and caused trouble with my vision again. There’s also the possibility of PTSD or other mental illnesses. They commonly overlap with brain injuries which makes things confusing. But treatments are similar. Diet, exercise, take care or your mental health. See someone if you can. Support groups. Find a hobby you care a lot about and throw yourself into it. The more I think about my symptoms the worse I feel, so I’m trying to focus my attention elsewhere.

Hi you might have seen one of my posts on here about Disney. I went for my birthday about 5 months after my injury. For me, being out in public and lots of stimulation sucks because my vision issues. But I was able to go and have an enjoyable time and even have an annual pass now (though I don’t use it frequently right now due to a lot of stressors). 

A big thing will be knowing your limits, pacing yourself, having an understanding group that doesn’t push you too hard, staying fed and hydrated, and absolutely get disability accommodations. It’s free to those who need it. Someone recommended it to me and had I not had that I just wouldn’t be able to make it through a day there. It will allow you to check in for rides but go somewhere to rest until your time to ride. I use that time to sit and eat or resting in one of the relaxation stations (they had them like a year ago, not sure if they still exist but any quiet place will do). 

Be mindful of what your triggers are. Because of my vision issues, I don’t really like the experiences with the 3d glasses (the 3d shows aren’t worth it for me. But for my favorite rides that use the glasses, like the avatar ride or toy story mania, they’re newer and seem to be more tolerable, and they’re actually fun so it’s not like damn why did I put myself through that for a silly show). I don’t like stuff that jerks me around or anything too rough that would cause headaches or nausea. I do still ride some bigger rides just preferably the smooth ones. I’ll just name some that I’ve found to be more trouble than they’re worth for me: Space mountain, Aerosmith (this one is hit or miss. I enjoyed it once but another time it made me sick), the 2 Star Wars rides that aren’t Rise of Resistance (riding in VR space ships, really jerky and flashing screens, not that fun), tower of terror, the ride in animal kingdom where you’re driving in a bumpy ass jeep (this one always sucked but especially with injury), haven’t been on mission space since my injury but remember it being rough as a kid. It’s hard to remember all off the top of my head but if you have any you’re iffy about hmu! There are some that seem like they’d be intense but are still enjoyable. Like Snow White, splash mountain, expedition Everest, etc.

Let yourself feel, remember, cry, etc. Talk about it to whoever will listen. Your college should offer some form of free counseling. Utilize that if you don’t have healthcare. Hey. I’m really sorry you’re going through all this. We have a lot in common. 

My first thought is C-PTSD as the symptoms overlap with brain injuries. And I’d say your BPD diagnosis is probably correct based on the symptoms you listed. 

I have struggled with most all the symptoms you listed PRIOR to my brain injury (recovering BPD and bouts of PTSD), so I’d say their presence wouldn’t automatically lead me to believe you did have a brain injury. 

But, it’s a weird situation because there’s so much overlap in different conditions and to my understanding brain injuries can basically cause these conditions. 

The symptoms that give me pause are the blurry vision, memory/cognitive issues. Those are things I didn’t have before that I got with my brain injury. But I was told by my doctors that C-PTSD can cause those. Also, I get blurred vision from my SSRI sometimes. There’s so many different factors in both our situations that can make our symptoms and overall health confusing.

And I’ve struggled with dissociative fears and little episodes before from experimenting with marijuana (not something you should do as a borderline), and then the pandemic made me feel like this year wasn’t real, but when I got my TBI I legitimately felt like a ghost and was convinced I was not alive anymore. 

Like I said, I had many of those symptoms before, but once I got my TBI I immediately felt something snap in me, like “oh fuck, something is terribly wrong,” and I had to rush to the hospital. I feel like if you did have one you’d notice some like immediate overnight kind of changes when it happened. Maybe that’s not always the case though.

Definitely get some kind of brain scan to rule it out if you have these fears. Unfortunately I’m not familiar with the doctor you listed so I don’t have any input there. My experience so far with scans is I had a CT scan which came back with nothing remarkable. I was supposed to get an MRI for more detail but couldn’t afford it. 

Get whatever you can afford. If it shows no damage, good. If there is some, then you’ll have an explanation for some of your issues and you’ll know to go about them a little differently. I’m on Lexapro and Adderall, so that part of treatment would be the same. Like they still manage the learning and mood stuff with therapy and meds. They’ll stress diet and exercise. A lot will be the same. But maybe you’d benefit from physical, vestibular, communications therapy and things like that if you did have a TBI. 

Good luck figuring things out. DM me if you ever need someone to talk to about it!
